paras: The Brighton train attack was an assault by about fifty striking iron workers on non-union laborers of the Joliet Iron and Steel Company aboard a Chicago & Alton train at Brighton, Chicago, on the evening of June 1, 1882. Most of those dragged out and beaten were Black workers, and a stray shot wounded Judge N. J. Pillsbury of the Illinois appellate court, a passenger. No one was reported killed, several men were arrested, and the story ran nationally within coverage of the iron strike.

For about two weeks the company had brought men from Joliet each day to unload iron at its Chicago docks, despite the strikers' efforts to stop it. The crew of about twenty non-union men, Black and white, were "scabs" to the strikers.

On the evening of June 1 the workers boarded the Dwight accommodation train at Bridgeport wharf, riding in a rear car added for them. When the train halted at the crossing of the Alton and Pan Handle lines at Brighton, about 5:30 or shortly before 6 o'clock, a crowd of men rushed out from hiding near the track. Four or five jumped onto the engine and held revolvers to the heads of the engineer and fireman, and others pulled the coupling pin.

Others entered the rear car and beat the workmen or pulled them out to the crowd, who beat, kicked and stamped on them with iron bars, clubs and stones. The wire counted half a dozen colored men and one white man beaten, the Chicago Times summary half a dozen Black men and a Swede with a fractured skull, and a longer Chicago account three Black men and one white laborer. Twenty-five or thirty shots were fired, and one struck Pillsbury, who had been playing euchre in the car, in the left hip.

Pillsbury was treated at the Washington Hotel in Chicago, where surgeons could not find the ball, and went home to Pontiac that night. The wounded workers went on to Joliet when the train resumed after forty minutes; police arrived after it left and found no one willing to say they could identify the attackers, though a dispatch the next day said none of the injured were likely to die.

Police made four or five arrests that night and held James O'Brien, John O'Neill and John Frawley on suspicion. By June 6 Eugene Reardon, out on bail, and a man named Murray had been identified as participants by one of the injured Black laborers. Their cases were continued in a justice's court on June 6 and remained unconcluded after a June 10 hearing; no later outcome appears in the coverage.

Chicago wire dispatches of June 1 ran the next day from Maine to Minnesota and Tennessee, usually within roundups of the iron strike. Headlines such as "Brutality Among Strikes," "Serious Riot" and "Bloody Work in Illinois" treated it as strike violence, and the main wire ended by saying the rioters dispersed "after beating the negroes to their hearts content." A separate wire, carried by the Omaha Bee and the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier, inflated the numbers to a hundred attackers and four Black men "fatally beaten," a claim later dispatches did not repeat.

In Illinois, the Ottawa Free Trader headed its summary "A Dastardly Outrage" and quoted the Chicago Times comparing the attackers to Missouri outlaws and "New Mexican cowboys." The Memphis Public Ledger's Chicago correspondent called it a "digraceful riot," while a long Chicago account reprinted in Tennessee remarked that if the beaten men "had been white men the strokes would undoubtedly have proved fatal."

Accounts placed the attack "five or six miles out," "fifty or sixty miles out" in the St. Paul Daily Globe's copy, and inside the city limits at Brighton; the last comes from the fuller Chicago reports. The wire blamed Pillsbury's wound on the rioters' gunfire; the Memphis correspondent called it accidental, and Daniel McWilliams, who was with him, said the shot came from inside the car. Three weeks later the Amalgamated Association's president, Jarrett, denied union responsibility and said the affair "grew out of the lawless conduct of some colored non-union iron workers from Joliet"; no other report describes such conduct.

accounts.label: Associated wire (Chicago, June 1)
accounts.gist: About fifty strikers stopped the train five or six miles out, pulled out half a dozen colored men and one white man and beat them; 25-30 shots, one wounding Pillsbury; no arrests.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee wire (Chicago, June 1)
accounts.gist: About 100 union strikers rushed through the cars attacking all passengers; four colored non-union men fatally beaten; twenty arrests by one o'clock.

accounts.label: Chicago papers, summarized and reprinted
accounts.gist: A planned ambush at the Brighton crossing; three negroes and a white laborer (or half a dozen negroes and a Swede) beaten with iron bars and stones; police arrived too late and found no willing witnesses.

accounts.label: Union president's claim
accounts.gist: Jarrett said the affair was not chargeable to union members and grew out of the lawless conduct of colored non-union workers from Joliet.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire inside strike roundups under heads such as 'Brutality Among Strikes', 'Serious Riot' and 'Bloody Work in Illinois'.
The Ottawa Free Trader headed it 'A Dastardly Outrage' and quoted the Chicago Times comparing it to Missouri and New Mexican cowboys.
The Memphis Public Ledger's Chicago correspondent called it a 'digraceful riot' and blamed immigration and labor 'hot heads'.
The Milan Exchange's Chicago account condemned the mob but remarked that if the beaten men 'had been white men the strokes would undoubtedly have proved fatal'.

info: Evening of Thursday, June 1, 1882; about 5:30 pm (Ottawa Free Trader/Chicago papers) or shortly before 6 pm (Milan Exchange's Chicago account)

Crossing of the Chicago & Alton and Pan Handle railroads at Brighton (Brighton Park, Brighton Station, near Western Avenue and Thirty-ninth Street), on the southwest edge of Chicago; described as inside the city limits, or about five miles out

About twenty non-union laborers of the Joliet Iron and Steel Company, white and Black, riding home to Joliet; those beaten were variously half a dozen colored men and one white man, three negroes and one white laborer, or half a dozen negroes and a Swede; none named. Judge N. J. Pillsbury of the appellate court, a passenger, was shot
Striking iron workers or dock hands and their friends, 'mostly young fellows'; unnamed and undisguised
